Healthcare Operations: Statistical Investigation of Encounter Costs¶

AnalystLab Africa Experience Lab · Week 3 · Track B (Data Science) · Intern: Nelson Nyamweya

Primary research question. How do recorded total claim costs differ across encounter classes, and how far are those differences associated with procedure activity, encounter duration and payer?

Why it matters. Encounter class (ambulatory, outpatient, wellness, urgent care, emergency, inpatient) is the most basic way a hospital plans capacity and budgets. If cost differences between classes are really driven by procedure activity or by who pays, then budgeting by class alone would mislead finance and operations managers.

Intended user. The hospital's operations and finance analytics team (revenue-cycle and service-line managers).

Decision supported. Which cost drivers to monitor and report alongside encounter class, and where payer coverage gaps should be investigated.

Evidence limits (summary). The data is synthetic (generated by the Synthea simulator for one hospital), covers 974 patients, has no medication or line-item detail, and many patients appear many times. Findings describe associations in this dataset, not causes, and are not clinical evidence. Full discussion in Section 8.

Notebook map. 1 Setup · 2 Load and inspect · 3 Data quality · 4 Preparation · 5 EDA · 6 Hypothesis tests · 7 Multivariable check and robustness · 8 Limitations · 9 Independent SQL reconciliation · 10 Summary

2. Load and inspect the datasets¶

The files are read with utf-8-sig because every CSV starts with a byte-order mark; read naively, the first column is named ﻿Id instead of Id, which silently breaks joins. The SQL setup script (create_hospital_db.sql) begins with DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS hospital_db; it was inspected but not run. The independent check in Section 9 uses a throwaway in-memory SQLite database instead.

In [2]:
def read(name, usecols=None):
    return pd.read_csv(RAW / f"{name}.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig", dtype={"ZIP": str}, usecols=usecols)

# Privacy by design: only the non-identifying patient columns are loaded. Names, addresses, birthplace and
# coordinates are never read into memory, so they cannot leak into any table, chart or export.
PAT_COLS = ["Id", "BIRTHDATE", "DEATHDATE", "MARITAL", "RACE", "ETHNICITY", "GENDER", "COUNTY"]
pat_header = pd.read_csv(RAW / "patients.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig", nrows=0).columns
enc_raw, pat_raw, proc_raw = read("encounters"), read("patients", PAT_COLS), read("procedures")
pay_raw, org_raw, dico = read("payers"), read("organizations"), read("data_dictionary")
tables = {"encounters": enc_raw, "patients": pat_raw, "procedures": proc_raw,
          "payers": pay_raw, "organizations": org_raw}
used = {"encounters": "Id, START, STOP, PATIENT, PAYER, ENCOUNTERCLASS, DESCRIPTION, BASE_ENCOUNTER_COST, TOTAL_CLAIM_COST, PAYER_COVERAGE",
        "patients": "Id, BIRTHDATE, DEATHDATE, GENDER (no names or addresses used)",
        "procedures": "ENCOUNTER, START, STOP, CODE, DESCRIPTION, BASE_COST",
        "payers": "Id, NAME", "organizations": "Id, NAME (context only)"}
overview = pd.DataFrame([{"table": k, "rows": len(v), "columns": len(pat_header) if k == "patients" else v.shape[1],
                          "fields_used": used[k]} for k, v in tables.items()])
save_tab(overview, "T01_table_overview")

3.3 Date, duration and cost consistency¶

In [7]:
enc["duration_h"] = (enc.STOP - enc.START).dt.total_seconds() / 3600
enc_after_death = enc.merge(pat[["Id", "DEATHDATE"]], left_on="PATIENT", right_on="Id", suffixes=("", "_p"))
after_death = (enc_after_death.START.dt.tz_localize(None).dt.normalize() > enc_after_death.DEATHDATE).sum()
proc_cost_per_enc = proc.groupby("ENCOUNTER").BASE_COST.sum()
enc["proc_cost"] = enc.Id.map(proc_cost_per_enc).fillna(0)
enc["other_cost"] = enc.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST - enc.BASE_ENCOUNTER_COST - enc.proc_cost

consistency = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Encounter START range", f"{enc.START.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {enc.START.max():%Y-%m-%d}"),

What these checks mean.

  • Duration is not a reliable length-of-stay measure. Most encounters have a fixed 15-minute duration, and 22,328 procedures start after their encounter's STOP time (median 1.4 h later, up to 182 days). STOP therefore marks the end of the encounter record, not the end of care. Duration is still analysed (H3) but with this caveat.
  • TOTAL_CLAIM_COST is not BASE + procedures. The dictionary says the total includes medications, immunisations and other line items that are not supplied, so only about 30% of encounters reconcile exactly. Some encounters have procedure lines costing more than the claim total, so procedure costs and claim totals were apparently generated independently: 5,086 encounters (18%) have procedure lines that cost more than the whole claim. We analyse TOTAL_CLAIM_COST as recorded and do not "fix" it.
  • BASE_ENCOUNTER_COST takes only five distinct values (a fixed tariff per encounter type), so it carries almost no information; TOTAL_CLAIM_COST is the meaningful outcome.
  • Encounters after death and zero-cost encounters are kept: they are few and removing them would require a rule we cannot verify. They are flagged in the processed file.
  • Missing REASONCODE (70% of encounters) is structural: the dictionary says it is filled "only if this encounter targeted a specific condition". It is not imputed. Missing DEATHDATE means the patient was alive at extract.

Encounters are not independent: ten patients generate about one fifth of all encounters. Statistical tests that treat every encounter as independent will overstate precision, so every hypothesis is re-checked with patient-level summaries or patient-clustered standard errors (Section 7).

4. Data preparation¶

All transformations are additive (new columns); no rows were removed from the analysis table.

In [9]:
pay_name = pay_raw.set_index("Id").NAME
enc["payer"] = enc.PAYER.map(pay_name)
public = {"Medicare", "Medicaid", "Dual Eligible"}
enc["payer_group"] = np.select([enc.payer.isin(public), enc.payer.eq("NO_INSURANCE")],
                               ["Public", "No insurance"], "Private")
enc["year"] = enc.START.dt.year
enc["quarter"] = enc.START.dt.tz_localize(None).dt.to_period("Q")
enc["n_procedures"] = enc.Id.map(proc.groupby("ENCOUNTER").size()).fillna(0).astype(int)
enc["has_procedure"] = enc.n_procedures > 0
enc["proc_band"] = pd.cut(enc.n_procedures, [-1, 0, 1, 3, np.inf], labels=["0", "1", "2-3", "4+"])
enc = enc.merge(pat[["Id", "BIRTHDATE", "DEATHDATE", "GENDER"]].rename(columns={"Id": "PATIENT"}), on="PATIENT", how="left")
enc["age"] = (enc.START.dt.tz_localize(None) - enc.BIRTHDATE).dt.days / 365.25
enc["age_band"] = pd.cut(enc.age, [-1, 17, 44, 64, 200], labels=["0-17", "18-44", "45-64", "65+"])
enc["over_24h"] = enc.duration_h > 24
enc["zero_coverage"] = enc.PAYER_COVERAGE == 0
enc["coverage_ratio"] = np.where(enc.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST > 0, enc.PAYER_COVERAGE / enc.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST, np.nan)
enc["log_cost"] = np.log1p(enc.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST)
enc["log_duration"] = np.log(enc.duration_h)
enc["flag_after_death"] = enc.START.dt.tz_localize(None).dt.normalize() > enc.DEATHDATE
enc["flag_zero_cost"] = enc.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST == 0
enc["class"] = pd.Categorical(enc.ENCOUNTERCLASS, CLASS_ORDER)
# Pseudonymous patient key: short sequential code instead of the source UUID (no names or addresses are ever loaded)
enc["patient_key"] = "P" + enc.PATIENT.astype("category").cat.codes.astype(str).str.zfill(4)

keep = ["Id", "patient_key", "START", "STOP", "year", "class", "DESCRIPTION", "payer", "payer_group", "GENDER", "age",
        "age_band", "duration_h", "over_24h", "BASE_ENCOUNTER_COST", "TOTAL_CLAIM_COST", "PAYER_COVERAGE",
        "coverage_ratio", "zero_coverage", "n_procedures", "has_procedure", "proc_band", "proc_cost", "other_cost",
        "flag_after_death", "flag_zero_cost"]
analysis = enc[keep + ["PATIENT", "log_cost", "log_duration", "quarter"]].copy()
analysis[keep].assign(START=lambda d: d.START.astype(str), STOP=lambda d: d.STOP.astype(str),
                      **{"class": lambda d: d["class"].astype(str), "age_band": lambda d: d.age_band.astype(str),
                         "proc_band": lambda d: d.proc_band.astype(str)}
                      ).to_parquet(PROC / "encounters_analysis.parquet", index=False)

cleaning_log = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Read CSVs with utf-8-sig", "Byte-order mark corrupted the first column name", "All rows"),
    ("START/STOP parsed to UTC datetimes", "Stored as ISO text", "All rows"),

What it shows. Volume rose from 1,336 encounters in 2011 to a peak of 3,885 in 2014, settled at about 2,200–2,500 a year from 2015 to 2020, and jumped to 3,530 in 2021. 2022 contains only five weeks and is excluded from trend charts. Ambulatory care is the largest class every year except 2021, when outpatient encounters doubled and overtook it (40%). What it cannot establish: with only 974 simulated patients, a handful of very frequent patients (Section 3.4) can move a whole year's count, so these swings are not evidence of changing demand in a real catchment population.

What it shows. Claim costs are extremely right-skewed (overall median $279 vs mean $3,640; skewness between 1.6 and 27.5 by class). Inpatient encounters have the highest median ($2,356) and wellness visits are second ($1,231), while emergency and urgent-care encounters have the lowest medians ($146 and $143), because most of them consist only of the flat base fee. Yet urgent care has the second-highest mean ($6,369): a minority of very expensive urgent care encounters pulls the mean up. Medians and means therefore tell different stories, and reporting averages alone would mislead. What it cannot establish: the box plots show differences but not whether they are larger than chance or what drives them (Section 6).

What it shows. The base encounter fee is only 2–5% of cost in every class; cost is driven by line items. Summed procedure line costs are close to, and in outpatient and wellness care larger than, the recorded claim totals, which confirms that the two fields were not generated to reconcile (Section 3.3). Procedure activity tracks the cost ranking: 92% of inpatient and 88% of wellness encounters include a procedure, but only 31% of emergency and 28% of urgent-care encounters do. This is the first sign that procedure activity, not the class label itself, may explain much of the cost difference (tested in H2 and Section 7). Limitation: because "other line items" are a residual, they cannot be broken down further, and for some classes procedure costs exceed the claim total (Section 3.3).

What it shows. 48.7% of encounters (13,586) have zero recorded payer coverage. This is driven almost entirely by payer, not by encounter class: uninsured encounters are 100% zero-coverage by definition, and four of the six private insurers (Anthem, Cigna, Aetna, Humana) record zero coverage on 96–100% of their encounters, while Medicare and Medicaid record coverage on over 99%. Zero coverage varies far less across encounter classes (33%–52%). Overall, payers cover only 30.6% of recorded claim cost, and uninsured encounters alone account for $49.3M of the $101.5M total (49%), with a median cost ($921) well above Medicare's ($235). What it cannot establish: whether "zero coverage" means a denied claim, an unpaid claim, a patient-pay plan, or simply a field the simulator did not populate for those insurers. There is no claim-status field, so this must be confirmed with the billing team before it is treated as lost revenue.

6. Hypotheses and statistical tests¶

Method choice. Costs are heavily skewed with unequal variances (Levene's test below), and groups are very unequal in size (1,135 inpatient vs 12,537 ambulatory). Mean-based tests (ANOVA, t-tests) would be dominated by a few extreme values, so the primary tests are rank-based (Kruskal–Wallis, Mann–Whitney, Spearman), with effect sizes reported alongside p-values because with n ≈ 28,000 even trivial differences are "significant". Encounter-level tests assume independence, which repeated patients violate, so every test is repeated on patient-level data in Section 7.

In [18]:
results = []

def eps_sq(H, n, k):
    return (H - k + 1) / (n - k)

groups = [analysis.loc[analysis["class"] == c, "TOTAL_CLAIM_COST"].values for c in CLASS_ORDER]
lev = stats.levene(*groups, center="median")
print(f"Brown–Forsythe (median-centred Levene) test of equal variances: W = {lev.statistic:.1f}, p = {lev.pvalue:.2e}")
print("Skewness by class:", {CLASS_LABEL[c]: round(stats.skew(g), 1) for c, g in zip(CLASS_ORDER, groups)})

Brown–Forsythe (median-centred Levene) test of equal variances: W = 159.2, p = 2.33e-167
Skewness by class: {'Ambulatory': np.float64(5.0), 'Outpatient': np.float64(3.8), 'Wellness': np.float64(2.9), 'Urgent care': np.float64(1.6), 'Emergency': np.float64(27.5), 'Inpatient': np.float64(11.6)}

H1. Total claim cost differs across encounter classes¶

  • H0: the distribution of TOTAL_CLAIM_COST is the same in all six encounter classes.
  • H1: at least one class has a stochastically higher or lower cost distribution.
  • Variables: TOTAL_CLAIM_COST (continuous, skewed) by ENCOUNTERCLASS (6 groups).
  • Method: Kruskal–Wallis H test, effect size ε²; Dunn post hoc comparisons with Holm correction.
  • Assumptions: independent observations (violated by repeat patients, checked in Section 7); ordinal or continuous outcome (met); similar distribution shapes if interpreting as a median difference (not met, so the result is read as a difference in distributions / mean ranks, with medians reported descriptively).
In [19]:
H, p = stats.kruskal(*groups)
e2 = eps_sq(H, len(analysis), len(CLASS_ORDER))
dunn = sp.posthoc_dunn(analysis.assign(c=analysis["class"].astype(str)), val_col="TOTAL_CLAIM_COST", group_col="c", p_adjust="holm")
dunn = dunn.loc[CLASS_ORDER, CLASS_ORDER]
dunn_long = [(CLASS_LABEL[a], CLASS_LABEL[b], dunn.loc[a, b]) for i, a in enumerate(CLASS_ORDER) for b in CLASS_ORDER[i + 1:]]
dunn_df = pd.DataFrame(dunn_long, columns=["class_a", "class_b", "p_holm"])
dunn_df["median_a"] = dunn_df.class_a.map({CLASS_LABEL[c]: desc.loc[c, "median"] for c in CLASS_ORDER})
dunn_df["median_b"] = dunn_df.class_b.map({CLASS_LABEL[c]: desc.loc[c, "median"] for c in CLASS_ORDER})
dunn_df["significant_0.05"] = dunn_df.p_holm < .05
save_tab(dunn_df.round(6), "T18_H1_dunn_posthoc")
results.append({"hypothesis": "H1 Cost differs across encounter classes", "test": "Kruskal–Wallis (6 groups)",
                "n": len(analysis), "statistic": f"H = {H:,.0f}", "p_value": p, "effect_size": f"ε² = {e2:.3f}",
                "decision": "Reject H0" if p < .05 else "Fail to reject H0"})
print(f"H = {H:,.1f}, df = 5, p = {p:.2e}, epsilon² = {e2:.3f}")
print(f"Non-significant pairs after Holm correction: {(~dunn_df['significant_0.05']).sum()} of {len(dunn_df)}")
dunn_df[~dunn_df["significant_0.05"]]

H = 2,025.2, df = 5, p = 0.00e+00, epsilon² = 0.072
Non-significant pairs after Holm correction: 2 of 15

class_a class_b p_holm median_a median_b significant_0.05
3 Ambulatory Emergency 0.937358 573.98 146.18 False
11 Wellness Inpatient 0.937358 1231.44 2355.59 False

Interpretation. Encounter class is associated with claim cost (p far below 0.001) with a medium effect (ε² = 0.072 at encounter level, 0.150 at patient level; benchmarks 0.01 small, 0.08 medium, 0.26 large). Class alone accounts for only about 7–15% of the variation in cost ranks, so most cost variation happens within classes. 13 of 15 pairs differ; the exceptions are ambulatory vs emergency and wellness vs inpatient. In plain language: inpatient and wellness encounters are typically the most expensive, ambulatory sits in the middle, and outpatient, emergency and urgent-care encounters are typically cheapest, although emergency and urgent care have long expensive tails. Practical significance: a budget that uses one average cost for all encounters would be badly wrong; costs need to be planned per class and the high-cost tail inside low-median classes (urgent care) needs its own monitoring. Limitation: this test says nothing about why classes differ; H2 and Section 7 address that.

H2. Encounters with recorded procedures cost more, within each encounter class¶

  • H0: within a given class, cost distributions are the same for encounters with and without a recorded procedure.
  • H1: encounters with ≥1 procedure have stochastically higher cost (one-sided).
  • Variables: TOTAL_CLAIM_COST by has_procedure, stratified by class (stratifying stops class differences from masquerading as a procedure effect).
  • Method: one-sided Mann–Whitney U in each class, Holm correction across the six tests; effect size = rank-biserial correlation r (= Cliff's δ); ratio of medians for practical size.
  • Assumptions: independent observations within and between groups (checked in Section 7); same-shaped distributions are not required for the stochastic-dominance reading used here.
In [20]:
h2 = []
for c in CLASS_ORDER:
    d = analysis[analysis["class"] == c]
    a, b = d.loc[d.has_procedure, "TOTAL_CLAIM_COST"], d.loc[~d.has_procedure, "TOTAL_CLAIM_COST"]
    u, pv = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="greater")
    r = 2 * u / (len(a) * len(b)) - 1
    h2.append({"class": CLASS_LABEL[c], "n_with": len(a), "n_without": len(b), "median_with": a.median(),
               "median_without": b.median(), "median_ratio": a.median() / b.median(), "U": u, "p_raw": pv,
               "rank_biserial_r": r})
h2 = pd.DataFrame(h2)
h2["p_holm"] = multipletests(h2.p_raw, method="holm")[1]
save_tab(h2.round(4), "T19_H2_procedure_vs_none_by_class")
results.append({"hypothesis": "H2 Encounters with procedures cost more (within class)",
                "test": "Mann–Whitney U ×6, one-sided, Holm", "n": len(analysis),
                "statistic": f"r from {h2.rank_biserial_r.min():.2f} to {h2.rank_biserial_r.max():.2f}",
                "p_value": h2.p_holm.max(), "effect_size": f"median ratio {h2.median_ratio.min():.1f}× to {h2.median_ratio.max():.1f}×",
                "decision": f"Reject H0 in {(h2.p_holm < .05).sum()} of 6 classes"})

Interpretation. In every class, encounters with a recorded procedure cost far more than those without — typically several times the median — and the effect sizes are large. Encounters without procedures cost little more than the base fee. Practical significance: procedure activity is the main cost lever inside every class, so monitoring "procedures per encounter" by class is more useful for cost control than tracking encounter counts alone. Limitation: a procedure is part of the cost by construction (it is a line item), so this confirms the billing mechanics rather than revealing a hidden cause; the operational question is which procedures and how often.

H3. Longer encounters have higher recorded claim costs¶

  • H0: ρ = 0 (no monotonic association between duration and cost) within a class.
  • H1: ρ ≠ 0.
  • Variables: duration_h and TOTAL_CLAIM_COST. Tested within the four classes where duration varies (wellness and urgent care have a constant 15-minute duration, so no test is possible).
  • Method: Spearman rank correlation (monotonic, robust to skew), plus partial Spearman controlling for number of procedures (because long encounters may simply contain more procedures). Holm correction.
  • Assumptions: independent pairs (checked in Section 7); monotonic rather than linear relationship. Heavy ties at 15 minutes reduce power and are handled by average ranks.
In [22]:
def partial_spearman(df, x, y, z):
    r = df[[x, y, z]].rank()
    rx = smf.ols(f"{x} ~ {z}", r).fit().resid
    ry = smf.ols(f"{y} ~ {z}", r).fit().resid
    return stats.pearsonr(rx, ry)

h3 = []
for c in ["ambulatory", "outpatient", "emergency", "inpatient"]:
    d = analysis[analysis["class"] == c]
    rho, pv = stats.spearmanr(d.duration_h, d.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST)
    pr_, ppv = partial_spearman(d, "duration_h", "TOTAL_CLAIM_COST", "n_procedures")
    h3.append({"class": CLASS_LABEL[c], "n": len(d), "pct_exactly_15min": (d.duration_h.round(3) == .25).mean(),
               "spearman_rho": rho, "p_raw": pv, "partial_rho_ctrl_procedures": pr_, "p_partial_raw": ppv})
h3 = pd.DataFrame(h3)
h3["p_holm"] = multipletests(h3.p_raw, method="holm")[1]
h3["p_partial_holm"] = multipletests(h3.p_partial_raw, method="holm")[1]
rho_all, p_all = stats.spearmanr(analysis.duration_h, analysis.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST)
save_tab(h3.round(4), "T20_H3_duration_vs_cost")
results.append({"hypothesis": "H3 Longer encounters cost more (within class)", "test": "Spearman ρ ×4 + partial ρ, Holm",
                "n": int(h3.n.sum()), "statistic": f"ρ from {h3.spearman_rho.min():.2f} to {h3.spearman_rho.max():.2f}",
                "p_value": h3.p_holm.max(), "effect_size": f"partial ρ {h3.partial_rho_ctrl_procedures.min():.2f} to {h3.partial_rho_ctrl_procedures.max():.2f}",
                "decision": f"Reject H0 in {(h3.p_holm < .05).sum()} of 4 testable classes"})

Interpretation. Duration and cost are positively associated in all four testable classes (ρ = 0.17 to 0.48), so H0 is rejected. But once the number of procedures is held constant the picture splits: in ambulatory (partial ρ = 0.26) and outpatient (0.42) care the association remains, while in emergency (−0.09) and inpatient (−0.05, not significant) care it disappears. Longer emergency and inpatient encounters cost more only because they contain more procedures. Practical significance: duration is a weak and unreliable cost signal in this data; procedure counts are more informative. Limitation: encounter STOP times do not mark the end of care (Section 3.3), and 69% of durations are a default 15 minutes, so this result should not be used to estimate a cost per hour.

H4. The share of encounters with zero payer coverage differs by encounter class¶

  • H0: zero coverage is independent of encounter class.
  • H1: the zero-coverage rate differs between classes.
  • Variables: zero_coverage (binary) × class (6 groups); then controlling for payer.
  • Method: χ² test of independence with Cramér's V; then a logistic regression of zero_coverage on class with payer fixed effects and patient-clustered standard errors, to see whether any class difference survives once payer is held constant. Uninsured encounters (always zero) are excluded from the adjusted model because they have no variation.
  • Assumptions: χ²: independent observations (violated by repeat patients; addressed by clustering in the logit), expected counts ≥5 in every cell (checked).

def or_table(m, label):
    t = pd.DataFrame({"odds_ratio": np.exp(m.params), "ci_low": np.exp(m.conf_int()[0]), "ci_high": np.exp(m.conf_int()[1]), "p": m.pvalues})
    t = t[t.index.str.contains("cls")]
    t.index = [CLASS_LABEL[i.split("T.")[1].rstrip("]")] for i in t.index]
    return t.add_prefix(label + "_")
h4_tab = or_table(logit_raw, "unadjusted").join(or_table(logit_adj, "payer_adjusted"))
wald = logit_adj.wald_test(" , ".join([f"{n} = 0" for n in logit_adj.params.index if "cls" in n]), scalar=True)
save_tab(ct.assign(zero_rate=ct[True] / ct.sum(axis=1)).round(3).reset_index().rename(columns={False: "covered", True: "zero_coverage"}), "T21_H4_zero_coverage_by_class")
save_tab(h4_tab.round(4).reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "class_vs_ambulatory"}), "T22_H4_logit_odds_ratios")
results.append({"hypothesis": "H4 Zero-coverage rate differs by encounter class", "test": "χ² independence; logit with payer FE, clustered SE",
                "n": len(analysis), "statistic": f"χ²({dof}) = {chi2:,.0f}; adjusted Wald χ² = {float(wald.statistic):,.1f}",

Interpretation. The χ² test rejects independence, but the effect is small (Cramér's V = 0.117). Adding payer to the model raises explained variation from a pseudo-R² of 0.04 to 0.81, confirming that who pays, not what type of encounter it is, determines whether coverage is recorded. A class effect remains after adjustment (Wald χ² = 37.7, p < 0.001), but its direction changes: emergency encounters look less likely to have zero coverage before adjustment (OR 0.38) and slightly more likely after (OR 1.47, not significant), because emergency patients are disproportionately on public payers, who almost always pay. This is a textbook confounding (Simpson's paradox) pattern and the reason raw class comparisons of coverage should not be reported on their own. Practical significance: coverage-gap investigations should be organised by payer contract, not by service line. Limitation: we cannot tell whether zero coverage is a denied claim or an unpopulated field.

7. Multivariable check and robustness¶

7.1 How much of the class difference is explained by procedures, payer and patient mix?¶

OLS on ln(1 + total claim cost) with encounter class, number of procedures (banded), log duration, payer group, age band, sex and year. Standard errors are clustered by patient, which corrects for repeated encounters. Coefficients are converted to approximate % differences in cost: (e^β − 1). This is an associational model, not a causal one.

In [25]:
m_df = analysis.assign(cls=analysis["class"].astype(str), procb=analysis.proc_band.astype(str), ageb=analysis.age_band.astype(str),
                       yr=analysis.year.astype(str), grp=analysis.PATIENT.astype("category").cat.codes)
f_class = "log_cost ~ C(cls, Treatment('ambulatory'))"
f_full = f_class + " + C(procb, Treatment('0')) + log_duration + C(payer_group, Treatment('Public')) + C(ageb, Treatment('18-44')) + C(GENDER) + C(yr)"
m1 = smf.ols(f_class, m_df).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": m_df.grp})
m2 = smf.ols(f_full, m_df).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": m_df.grp})

def pct_tab(m):
    ci = m.conf_int()
    t = pd.DataFrame({"pct_diff": np.expm1(m.params) * 100, "ci_low": np.expm1(ci[0]) * 100, "ci_high": np.expm1(ci[1]) * 100, "p": m.pvalues})
    return t.drop("Intercept")

cmp.index = [CLASS_LABEL[i.split("T.")[1].rstrip("]")] for i in cmp.index]

Interpretation. Encounter class alone explains 4.3% of the variance in log cost; adding procedures, payer, age, sex, year and duration raises R² to 0.60. Procedure activity is by far the strongest term (one recorded procedure goes with roughly 24× the cost of none). Adjustment changes the class picture in two directions:

  • Wellness's premium mostly disappears (+141% → +23%): wellness visits cost more mainly because they include more procedures (4.8 on average).
  • Emergency and urgent care flip from "cheap" to "expensive" (−9% → +158% and +2% → +76%): their low raw medians come from the many encounters with no procedure; when procedures do occur, they are costlier than in ambulatory care.
  • Uninsured encounters cost about 36% more than comparable public-payer encounters, and costs are lower for patients aged 45+ than for 18–44 once procedures are held constant.

Duration's coefficient turns negative once class and procedures are in the model (VIF 4.1, the highest), which again shows duration is not a dependable cost signal here. All VIFs are below 5. The residuals are reasonably symmetric on the log scale, with heavier tails than normal; clustered standard errors do not rely on normality for large samples. This is still an association model: unmeasured factors (diagnosis, severity, medications) could explain the remaining differences.

7.2 Robustness to repeated patients and outliers¶

Three checks: (a) re-run H1–H3 on patient-level data (each patient contributes one median value per class, so frequent patients cannot dominate); (b) cluster bootstrap of the class medians, resampling whole patients (1,000 resamples); (c) re-run H1 after removing the top 1% of costs and after excluding the three most frequent patients.

    ("H1", "Patient level: one median per patient per class", len(pl), f"H = {H_pl:,.0f}", p_pl, f"ε² = {e2_pl:.3f}"),
    ("H1", "Top 1% of costs removed (>${:,.0f})".format(cut), len(trim), f"H = {H_tr:,.0f}", p_tr, f"ε² = {eps_sq(H_tr, len(trim), 6):.3f}"),
    ("H1", "Three most frequent patients removed", len(nt), f"H = {H_nt:,.0f}", p_nt, f"ε² = {eps_sq(H_nt, len(nt), 6):.3f}"),
    ("H2", "Patient level: paired Wilcoxon, with vs without procedure (same patient & class)", len(pe), f"W = {w_stat:,.0f}", w_p,
     f"{(pe[True] > pe[False]).mean():.0%} of pairs higher with procedure"),
    ("H3", "Patient level: Wilcoxon on each patient's own duration–cost ρ", len(h3_pl), f"median ρ = {h3_pl.median():.2f}", p_h3,
     f"{(h3_pl > 0).mean():.0%} of patients have ρ > 0"),
    ("H4", "Logit with payer fixed effects, patient-clustered SE (insured only)", int(logit_adj.nobs), f"Wald χ² = {float(wald.statistic):,.1f}",
     float(wald.pvalue), f"pseudo-R² {logit_raw.prsquared:.3f} → {logit_adj.prsquared:.3f}"),
], columns=["hypothesis", "check", "n", "statistic", "p_value", "effect"])
rob["p_value"] = rob.p_value.map(lambda v: "< 0.001" if v < .001 else f"{v:.3f}")
save_tab(rob, "T28_robustness_checks")

fig.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "F10_bootstrap_medians")

Interpretation. The conclusions hold under every robustness check: the class effect remains large at patient level, after trimming outliers and after removing the most frequent patients; the procedure effect holds when each patient is compared with themselves; and payer remains the dominant driver of zero coverage. The bootstrap intervals for inpatient care are very wide ($1,187 to $10,830) because a few patients account for many inpatient stays, which is exactly the repeated-patient effect the brief asks us to consider. Some intervals collapse onto a single value (outpatient $278.58) because claim totals cluster on a few tariff amounts, another sign of simulated pricing.

8. Limitations¶

  • Synthetic data. All records are generated by Synthea for a single (real-named) hospital. Prices follow a simulator tariff (five base fees, many procedures with one fixed price). Findings describe this dataset, not the real Massachusetts General Hospital or any African health system.
  • Missing cost components. Medications, immunisations and other line items are in TOTAL_CLAIM_COST but not supplied, so 70% of encounters cannot be reconciled to their components, and some have procedure costs above the claim total.
  • Unreliable duration. STOP does not mark the end of care; 69% of durations are a default 15 minutes.
  • Repeated records. 974 patients produce 27,891 encounters; the top 10 patients produce ~20%. Encounter-level p-values are optimistic; patient-level and clustered checks were added.
  • Unequal groups. Inpatient (1,135) vs ambulatory (12,537); rank tests and effect sizes are used, and class-level medians come with bootstrap intervals.
  • Confounding. Diagnosis, severity and medications are not available (REASONCODE is missing for 70%), so class and procedure effects may partly reflect patient need. Payer confounds class–coverage comparisons.
  • Coverage meaning. Zero coverage cannot be split into denial, non-submission, self-pay or unpopulated field.
  • Partial periods. 2022 has five weeks of data; 2011 starts on 2 January.
  • Association, not causation. None of the tests show that changing a class, procedure count or duration would change cost. A procedure is mechanically part of the claim.

9. Independent reconciliation with SQL (validation)¶

Key figures are recomputed from the raw CSVs in an isolated in-memory SQLite database using SQL written independently of the pandas pipeline (no shared code), following the reference questions in hospital_analytics_questions.sql. The MySQL setup script is not executed.

In [30]:
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
for t in ["encounters", "procedures", "payers", "patients"]:
    pd.read_csv(RAW / f"{t}.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig", dtype=str).to_sql(t, con, index=False)
sql_dir = ROOT / "sql"
q = {}
q["total_encounters"] = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters"
q["zero_coverage_encounters"] = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters WHERE CAST(PAYER_COVERAGE AS REAL) = 0"
q["over_24h_encounters"] = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters WHERE (julianday(STOP) - julianday(START)) * 24 > 24"
q["total_claim_cost_sum"] = "SELECT ROUND(SUM(CAST(TOTAL_CLAIM_COST AS REAL)), 2) FROM encounters"
q["inpatient_encounters"] = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters WHERE ENCOUNTERCLASS = 'inpatient'"
q["encounters_with_procedure"] = "SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ENCOUNTER) FROM procedures"
q["medicare_avg_total_claim_cost"] = ("SELECT ROUND(AVG(CAST(e.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST AS REAL)), 2) FROM encounters e "
                                       "JOIN payers p ON e.PAYER = p.Id WHERE p.NAME = 'Medicare'")
q["encounters_2014"] = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters WHERE substr(START, 1, 4) = '2014'"
q["most_frequent_procedure_count"] = "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM procedures GROUP BY DESCRIPTION ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 1"
py_vals = {
    "total_encounters": len(analysis), "zero_coverage_encounters": int(analysis.zero_coverage.sum()),
    "over_24h_encounters": int(analysis.over_24h.sum()), "total_claim_cost_sum": round(analysis.TOTAL_CLAIM_COST.sum(), 2),
    "inpatient_encounters": int((analysis["class"] == "inpatient").sum()), "encounters_with_procedure": int(analysis.has_procedure.sum()),
    "medicare_avg_total_claim_cost": round(cov_payer.loc["Medicare", "avg_total_claim_cost"], 2),
    "encounters_2014": int(yv.loc[2014]), "most_frequent_procedure_count": int(proc_stats.times_performed.iloc[0]),
}
recon = pd.DataFrame([{"metric": k, "pandas": py_vals[k], "sql": con.execute(s).fetchone()[0]} for k, s in q.items()])
recon["match"] = [abs(float(a) - float(b)) < 0.01 for a, b in zip(recon.pandas, recon.sql)]
save_tab(recon, "T29_sql_reconciliation")
(sql_dir).mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(sql_dir / "validation_queries_sqlite.sql").write_text("-- Independent validation queries (SQLite). Run against the raw CSVs loaded as tables.\n\n" +
                                                      "\n\n".join(f"-- {k}\n{s};" for k, s in q.items()) + "\n")
assert recon.match.all(), "pandas and SQL disagree"
recon

9.1 Answers to the reference SQL questions (for completeness)¶

Return visits within 30 days are counted from one encounter's STOP to the same patient's next START. This is labelled a 30-day return encounter, not a clinical readmission: Synthea schedules many routine follow-ups (e.g. dialysis sessions), so most returns are planned care.

In [31]:
ref = {}
ref["a_encounters_per_year"] = yv.to_dict()
cls_year = pd.crosstab(analysis.year, analysis["class"], normalize="index").round(3)
save_tab(cls_year.reset_index(), "T30_class_share_by_year")
ref["c_pct_over_24h"] = round(analysis.over_24h.mean() * 100, 2)
ref["2a_zero_coverage"] = f"{int(analysis.zero_coverage.sum()):,} ({analysis.zero_coverage.mean():.1%})"
uq = analysis.groupby("quarter").PATIENT.nunique()
save_tab(uq.rename("unique_patients").reset_index().assign(quarter=lambda d: d.quarter.astype(str)), "T31_unique_patients_per_quarter")
s = analysis.sort_values(["PATIENT", "START"])
s["next_start"] = s.groupby("PATIENT").START.shift(-1)
s["gap_days"] = (s.next_start - s.STOP).dt.total_seconds() / 86400
ret = s[(s.gap_days >= 0) & (s.gap_days <= 30)]
ref["3b_patients_with_30day_return"] = int(ret.PATIENT.nunique())
ref["3b_30day_return_encounters"] = len(ret)
ret_after_inpatient = s[(s["class"] == "inpatient") & (s.gap_days >= 0) & (s.gap_days <= 30)]
ref["3b_patients_with_return_within_30d_of_inpatient_stay"] = int(ret_after_inpatient.PATIENT.nunique())
top_ret = ret.groupby("patient_key").size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5)
save_tab(top_ret.rename("return_encounters_30d").reset_index(), "T32_top5_patients_30day_returns_pseudonymised")
print(json.dumps({k: (v if not isinstance(v, dict) else {str(a): b for a, b in v.items()}) for k, v in ref.items()}, indent=1))
